extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, literary critics, and educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, eighteenth‑century guidance on writing style, memory/attention for reading and composition, and principles for fair literary criticism. Emphasizes matching diction to audience, authenticity in depiction, and the balance between rules and genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspicuity does not come from mere easiness of language but from using the right terms to delineate parts; technical terms are proper when one examines or analyzes a subject in depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specialized vocabulary when you are analyzing parts of an art or addressing an expert audience; avoid omitting necessary terms when precise delineation is required. Recognize that such terms may displease general readers only because few have examined the subject closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction to audience and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of expression are proper depending on how cursorily a subject is surveyed or how accurately it is examined (e.g., casuistic morality vs directing common practice; farmer instruction vs philosophical explanation of vegetation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt vocabulary, complexity, and detail to the reader's needs and the writer's purpose: use plain language for practical instruction and more technical or learned terms when addressing specialists or conducting analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth over superficial ease
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity or apparent easiness of language can indicate shallowness of thought; real perspicuity may require technical or precise language rather than artificial simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate simple or popular diction with intellectual depth. If a subject demands precision, prefer exact terms even if they are less familiar; avoid flattening complex thought into platitudes for the sake of seeming easy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in depiction (avoid pastoral affectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid romanticized, second‑hand images of rural life; pastoral tropes (shepherdesses dancing, swains piping) may come from authors rather than observation and lead to unrealistic portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base depictions on observation and accurate detail rather than borrowed poetic clichés. If an author projects an idealized scene without experience, the result will ring false—readers will notice incongruity between language and reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate social and material detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes and characters should reflect believable economic and social realities (e.g., country produce could be dearer than in town; farmers have different habits and priorities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include realistic, plausible facts about daily life, costs, customs, and behaviors to ground scenes. Small economic or social inaccuracies undermine credibility and reveal authorial ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The true art of memory is attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention depends chiefly on attention: reading with delight secures attention and thus memory, while distraction or overfull minds prevent impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate focused, attentive reading and study. Prioritize clear, undistracted concentration over mechanical mnemonic tricks; pleasurable engagement with material improves retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer repetition and focused reading to mechanical transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying passages into commonplace books is less effective than reading and re‑reading with attention; the hand does not bind memory more closely than the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid spending excessive time transcribing texts that can be consulted; use repeated, attentive reading and scheduled review rather than wholesale copying or marginalia that interrupt comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment and purposeful activity as cure for intrusive thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Forgetfulness (the ability to dismiss useless or afflicting thoughts) is aided by resolute reason and by occupying the mind with present tasks; idleness fosters gloomy retrospection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or working, maintain purposeful engagement with present tasks to avoid destructive rumination. For writers, disciplined activity keeps imagination productive and prevents paralysing dwelling on the past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should judge the whole, not only parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics who judge only by parts or by inferior beauties misestimate works of genius because they cannot comprehend the whole; judging by parts yields incomplete or misleading evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, attempt to perceive its overall design and effect before condemning or praising isolated elements. Avoid letting expertise in minor rules substitute for a grasp of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance rules with natural perception in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules are useful but not absolute; a servile attention to minute rules can be inconsistent with higher excellence, and genius may lie beyond codified rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal rules as guides, not inflexible measures. Train immediate literary perception (taste, natural sensibility) alongside knowledge of rules, and allow for exceptions where artistic effect demands them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial connoisseurship and cant
rubrics_metrics.description: A superficial 'connoisseur' who parrots names and academy rules without ideas offers only cant—volubility of terms without attached meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate genuine understanding rather than performative name‑dropping. Ensure that references to artists, schools, or principles serve analysis and insight rather than rhetorical polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect genre‑specific appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities that are virtues in one class of art may be faults in another (e.g., Rubens' harmony or Rembrandt's chiaroscuro might detract from Raffaelle's dignity; the sprightly turn of an epigram ill suits heroic poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess or compose works relative to the conventions, aims, and appropriate qualities of their genre. Do not import standards of one genre wholesale into another; tailor technique to desired effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy poetry: natural thought, undistorted diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Easy poetry expresses natural thoughts without violence to language: avoid harsh or daring figures, transpositions, unusual acceptations of words, artifices of verse construction, unnecessary epithets, needless repetition, and uncommon syntactic structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for diction and syntax that sound natural and unobtrusive; remove any epithet or construction that can be dropped without loss of sense. Treat any appearance of artifice as impairing the grace of 'easy' verse. Beware affectation and fashionable phrases that imitate ease but are actually contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scrupulosity that kills higher excellency
rubrics_metrics.description: An over‑fastidious, rule‑bound criticism which insists on minute exactness can be inconsistent with and destructive of true genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate attention to technical correctness with openness to the whole work's spirit; do not let pedantic exactness prevent recognition of bold or original merit.
